identity.title: Proximal symmetric weakness (chair-rise/Gowers-type maneuver, arm abduction) without focal deficit

technique.how: Ask the patient to rise from a chair with arms crossed, step onto a stool, and abduct the arms overhead against resistance; compare with distal power (grip, dorsiflexion) and grade MRC 0-5 bilaterally in shoulder abduction, elbow flexion, wrist extension, hip flexion, knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion (sum score 0-60). Check reflexes and sensation for focal or length-dependent deficit.
technique.prerequisites: Alert, cooperative patient able to follow commands; document pain that limits effort and recent drugs (statins, steroids, colchicine), alcohol and electrolytes.
technique.contraindications: Do not test chair-rise in patients at fall risk without assistance.

interpretation.positive_finding: Symmetric proximal weakness with preserved sensation and reflexes suggests myopathy (inflammatory, toxic/statin, endocrine, hypokalemia/hypophosphatemia) or ICU-acquired/deconditioning weakness; MRC sum score <48 defines significant weakness in the ICU literature.
interpretation.negative_finding: Normal proximal power argues against a generalized myopathy or electrolyte myopathy; distal or asymmetric weakness or areflexia points instead to neuropathy, GBS, or focal CNS/cord lesions.
interpretation.pitfalls: Pain, delirium, sedation and poor effort mimic weakness; GBS may begin proximally and be areflexic, so always test reflexes. Neuromuscular junction disease (myasthenia) produces fatigable proximal and bulbar weakness.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: check K, phosphate, CK, TSH, drug/alcohol review; consider EMG. Asymmetric, distal, areflexic or with sensory level: pursue GBS/cord/stroke pathways urgently.

sources.citation: Hermans G, Clerckx B, Vanhullebusch T, Segers J, Vanpee G, Robbeets C, Casaer MP, Wouters P, et al. Interobserver agreement of Medical Research Council sum-score and handgrip strength in the intensive care unit. Muscle Nerve. 2012.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not attribute weakness to deconditioning when there is a sensory level, bladder dysfunction, bulbar symptoms, respiratory weakness or rapidly ascending course.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Ascending weakness, areflexia, dysphagia or falling vital capacity requires urgent GBS/neuromuscular respiratory assessment; severe hypokalemia can cause paralysis and arrhythmia.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: In the ICU, MRC sum-score interobserver ICC was 0.95 (0.92-0.97); kappa for 'significant weakness' (MRC sum-score <48) was 0.68 +/- 0.09 and for 'severe weakness' (<36) 0.93 +/- 0.07 (Hermans 2012, Abstract).

extraction_notes: No diagnostic-accuracy study of proximal symmetric weakness as a sign for myopathy, electrolyte weakness or GBS versus other causes was found; status not_quantified. Hermans 2012 is a reliability study only: 'The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for MRC sum-score was 0.95 (0.92-0.97)' and kappa 'was 0.68 +/- 0.09, 0.88 +/- 0.07, and 0.93 +/- 0.07, respectively' for MRC <48, upper-limb subtotal <24, and MRC <36 (Abstract). PubMed search 'proximal muscle weakness myopathy diagnostic accuracy physical examination' returned only a small SMA fasciculation study (PMID 35879189), not relevant to this sign. The MRC <48 threshold for ICU-acquired weakness comes from the Hermans abstract.
